clauses.statement: The second create and the tag-mismatched replace both lose, which is 2 attempts the endpoint rejects before the capability counts as demonstrated.

clauses.subject: bytes-are-read-back
clauses.statement: The sentinel is read back after the losing writes and its bytes are compared against what the winning create wrote. A backend that answers success while ignoring the precondition is caught here and nowhere else.

clauses.subject: inconclusive-outcome
clauses.statement: An unsupported-method response, a forbidden response from a read-only credential, and a transport error each raise `SyncProbeInconclusive`, and every one of them reads as capability not demonstrated.

clauses.subject: coordination-setting
clauses.statement: `[sync] coordination` takes `cas` or `single-writer`. Left unset, the resolved mode derives from the probe outcome.

clauses.subject: declared-cas-undemonstrated
clauses.statement: Naming `cas` against a backend whose probe did not demonstrate the capability raises `SyncCoordinationUnproven` and the push stops rather than degrading to an unserialized write.

clauses.subject: single-writer-skips-the-probe
clauses.statement: Declaring `single-writer` performs no probe at all, costing no round trip and requiring no write permission on the probe path.

clauses.subject: read-only-credential-lands-on-the-machine-lease
clauses.statement: A capable backend reached with a credential that cannot write returns an inconclusive probe, and that deployment coordinates through the per-machine lease instead of the bucket lease.

clauses.subject: probe-runs-once
clauses.statement: The probe runs once per process at startup and its outcome is held for the life of that process.

clauses.subject: sentinel-does-not-persist
clauses.statement: The sentinel is deleted at the end of a successful probe, and a sentinel left behind by an interrupted probe is overwritten by the next one rather than read as state.

clauses.subject: resolved-mode-is-reported
clauses.statement: `contextful sync diagnose` reports the resolved mode, the probe outcome that produced it, and whether the setting or the measurement decided.

clauses.subject: commit-is-compare-and-set
clauses.statement: The index commit is a compare-and-set over a merge of the remote index. A writer losing the race re-reads, re-merges and re-commits rather than replacing the winner's entries.

clauses.subject: scoped-union
clauses.statement: The remote contributes an entry to the merged index where this writer has never written, and nowhere else.

clauses.subject: foreign-key-shapes
clauses.statement: Three key shapes count as another writer's: a run directory whose node segment is another node id, a request-ledger filename carrying another node id, and any key outside those trees that this writer's own index does not name.

clauses.subject: deletion-propagates
clauses.statement: An entry this writer owns and no longer holds locally drops out of the merged index, which is how snapshot garbage collection and run retention reach a consumer.

clauses.subject: commit-retries
clauses.statement: `[sync] push_retries` bounds the re-read-and-re-commit loop at 5 attempts.

clauses.subject: retries-exhausted
clauses.statement: Exhausting the commit retries raises `SyncManifestRebaseExhausted`, reports that every uploaded object is already in the bucket, and asks for a re-run rather than committing an index it did not rebase.

clauses.subject: merge-runs-in-both-modes
clauses.statement: The merge is performed under both coordination modes. The compare-and-set is the part that makes a concurrent commit safe, not the part that makes the union correct.

clauses.subject: run-objects-union
clauses.statement: Run files and request-ledger files union across writers, their identifiers being unique and their paths or filenames carrying the writing node.

clauses.subject: snapshot-objects-take-the-local-side
clauses.statement: Snapshot entries resolve to this writer's, one writer owning a table's snapshot tier as a unit and a snapshot being a recomputable fold over run files the union already carries.

clauses.subject: catalog-resolves-at-the-key
clauses.statement: Catalog entries resolve to this writer's at the key level, the catalog being a cache each machine reconstructs from the tree.

clauses.subject: schemas-reconcile-on-the-next-write
clauses.statement: Table schema objects carry no merge rule of their own: two writers' schemas reconcile when the next write lands and reconciliation runs over the merged shape.

clauses.subject: cursor-by-recency
clauses.statement: A cursor entry resolved by whichever copy was written last raises `SyncCursorConflict`. A cursor resolves by its declared kind, which permits no concurrent advance that skips records.

clauses.subject: every-owned-tier-has-an-arm
clauses.statement: Each writer-owned tier carries its own ownership arm in the merge. A key shape falling through to the unowned default is one whose local deletion reaches no consumer, so the request ledger spells its node in the filename rather than in a path segment.

clauses.subject: grant-projected-section
clauses.statement: The sync edge projects the per-table section of the bucket manifest by the same table grants as the file list, so a capability-scoped replica reads no other table's contract metadata.

clauses.subject: consumer-reads-the-index-alone
clauses.statement: A bucket consumer asserts contract identity and derives staleness from the bucket manifest against its own clock, with no engine in the loop.

clauses.subject: offline-manifest-emit
clauses.statement: `contextful sync manifest --emit <path>` writes the same section offline, so a consumer's gate asserts against a producer-generated artifact ahead of any bucket existing.

clauses.subject: node-id-resolution-order
clauses.statement: A machine's writer node id resolves once per process: `CONTEXTFUL_NODE_ID`, then `[node] id` in the project configuration, then a random `node-<8 hex>` generated once and persisted.

clauses.subject: node-id-state-path
clauses.statement: The generated node id persists at `$CONTEXTFUL_STATE_DIR`, else `$XDG_STATE_HOME/contextful`, else the platform user-state directory for the process owner.

clauses.subject: node-id-sits-outside-the-store-root
clauses.statement: The node id is persisted outside the store root, so copying a store onto a second machine carries no identity with it and two machines never present one holder.

clauses.subject: node-id-length
clauses.statement: A node id spans 64 chars at most.

clauses.subject: node-id-shape
clauses.statement: A resolved node id the path-safe pattern rejects raises `SyncNodeIdInvalid` at process start, ahead of a key, a lease object or a run directory carrying that value.

clauses.subject: node-id-under-control-plane-config
clauses.statement: A node id declared in a control-plane configuration raises `SyncNodeIdShared`, a control-plane snapshot being applied to every machine reconciling it.

clauses.subject: one-port-two-implementations
clauses.statement: Leasing sits behind one port with two implementations, selected by the resolved coordination mode and by whether a bucket is configured.

clauses.subject: machine-lease-is-the-default
clauses.statement: The default lease is a row in the machine's own catalog, which serializes processes on that machine and nothing beyond it.

clauses.subject: bucket-lease-object
clauses.statement: The bucket lease is a sentinel object at `leases/<pipeline_id>.json` carrying the holder's node id, the acquisition instant, the expiry instant and the fencing token.

clauses.subject: acquisition-is-a-conditional-create
clauses.statement: A bucket lease is taken with a conditional create, so two machines reaching an unheld pipeline at once produce one holder and one loser.

clauses.subject: renewal-is-tag-checked
clauses.statement: A renewal and a steal are both a conditional replace against the entity tag just read. The tag check is what makes noticing an expiry and taking the lease one indivisible step between two machines that notice together.

clauses.subject: ttl
clauses.statement: A lease is granted for 10 min and expires without action from anyone.

clauses.subject: renewal-interval
clauses.statement: A holder renews every 200 s, a third of the granted life, so a seed or a backfill running longer than one grant keeps its hold mid-write.

clauses.subject: held-lease
clauses.statement: A run finding an unexpired lease raises `LeaseHeld`, naming the holder and the expiry instant, is skipped, and is attempted again on the next reconciliation tick.

clauses.subject: expiry-frees-a-crashed-holder
clauses.statement: A lease left behind by a machine that stopped expires on its own, so a crash locks nobody out past the granted life.

clauses.subject: fencing-token
clauses.statement: Acquisition yields a fencing token that increases monotonically per pipeline, and the holder stamps it on each object it commits under that pipeline.

clauses.subject: stale-fence
clauses.statement: A commit whose fencing token is below the one the lease object carries raises `LeaseFenced`, so a holder that paused past its expiry lands nothing after a successor took over.

clauses.subject: release-by-a-non-holder
clauses.statement: Releasing a lease whose holder is another node id raises `LeaseNotHeld` and leaves the object untouched.

clauses.subject: cursor-object
clauses.statement: The committed cursor position rides at `cursors/<pipeline_id>.json` beside the lease it belongs to.

clauses.subject: cursor-travels-with-the-lease
clauses.statement: A cursor position is written at release and adopted at acquisition, so the next holder resumes from where its predecessor stopped rather than from a private position of its own.

clauses.subject: wrong-cursor-kind-in-the-prefix
clauses.statement: A cursor value whose kind takes no lease, reaching the `cursors/` prefix, raises `LeaseCursorKindMismatch`; the values that live there are the ones a single writer has to agree on.

clauses.subject: unresolved-node-id
clauses.statement: The bucket lease refuses the fallback node id `local` by name, raising `LeaseNodeIdLocal`, keeping that machine on the per-machine lease and logging the environment variable that fixes it.

clauses.subject: holder-identity-is-the-node-id
clauses.statement: A lease holder is identified by node id alone, so re-entrancy is scoped to one machine and two machines presenting one identity is the failure the identity rules exclude.

clauses.subject: one-compaction-owner
clauses.statement: Compaction is the operation that is not append-only, and exactly one machine owns compaction for a store.

clauses.subject: second-compaction-owner
clauses.statement: A compaction pass started on a machine the store does not name as its compaction owner raises `SyncCompactionNotOwned`. Two machines folding one table at once is the path by which committed rows are lost.

clauses.subject: three-mechanisms-for-a-second-writer
clauses.statement: A bucket written from more than one machine holds three mechanisms together: reconcile before a run, a bucket-held write lease, and a rebase of the index on a losing commit. Any one of them alone leaves a writer publishing an index that omits the other's objects.

clauses.subject: lease-state-stays-local
clauses.statement: Lease and cursor state in the machine's catalog is never overwritten by a reconcile, that file being excluded from the objects a pull-before-run fetches.

clauses.subject: replica-is-read-only
clauses.statement: A replica originates nothing it holds: its catalog comes back from the objects it pulled, the canonical store stays the one authority for every table it serves, and a write travels there rather than landing on the replica.

clauses.subject: write-through-a-replica
clauses.statement: A write verb invoked against a replica raises `ReplicaWriteRefused`, naming the canonical store the deployment configuration points at.

clauses.subject: refresh-is-a-diff
clauses.statement: A refresh fetches the top-level index, diffs it against local digests, downloads the changed snapshot directories together with their sidecars, and swaps the current-snapshot pointer.

clauses.subject: absence-costs-one-snapshot
clauses.statement: A replica returning after a long absence fetches one current snapshot per affected table rather than the history in between, the refresh being a diff of content digests rather than a replay of commits.

clauses.subject: pointer-swap-is-indivisible
clauses.statement: The current-snapshot pointer moves in one step, and a query already running finishes against the pointer it started on.

clauses.subject: partial-parquet
clauses.statement: A replica holding a strict subset of a snapshot's Parquet raises `ReplicaPartialParquet` at refresh. Data files of one snapshot arrive together or the snapshot stays unpublished on that replica.

clauses.subject: sidecar-subset-is-legal
clauses.statement: A replica legitimately holds a subset of a snapshot's sidecar indexes, each sidecar being derivable from the data files beside it.

clauses.subject: missing-sidecar
clauses.statement: A query needing an index or a partition the replica does not hold raises `ReplicaMissingIndex` and names the refresh that supplies it, rather than answering from what is present.

clauses.subject: sensitive-tables-are-off-by-default
clauses.statement: A table declaring sensitive columns carries replicate-off by default, so the ordinary refresh moves no copy of it onto a consumer machine.

clauses.subject: sensitive-table-direct
clauses.statement: A refresh requesting a replicate-off table raises `ReplicaSensitiveTable`, and a consumer needing those columns reads them through the proxying face instead of holding the files.

clauses.subject: proxying-face
clauses.statement: The proxying face answers over the canonical store: it verifies the presented credential, returns projected rows rather than file handles, and records each read.

clauses.subject: rebuild-what-is-not-received
clauses.statement: A replica reconstructs its run bookkeeping from the file tree with `contextful context rebuild-catalog`, the read path having discovered each committed run by its marker file already.

clauses.subject: replica-loses-nothing-unrebuildable
clauses.statement: Everything a replica does not receive is derivable from the objects it does receive, so a refusal to ship the cache costs a rebuild and no data.

clauses.subject: object-selection-follows-the-grant
clauses.statement: A replica's object selection is driven by the table patterns its pulling credential carries, the same matcher that decides which tables register as relations for a caller.

clauses.subject: connection-views
clauses.statement: Ahead of a statement the engine opens a connection and issues one create-or-replace view per table directory the manifests name, each source resolved at that moment. No view directory exists on disk, so nothing regenerates and no fingerprint drifts.

clauses.subject: file-list
clauses.statement: A registered relation receives an explicit, sorted list of part files rather than a glob pattern. What a relation reads is decided by the manifests, never by whatever happens to sit in the directory when the scan starts.

clauses.subject: engine
clauses.statement: The executor is an embedded columnar SQL engine linked into every binary target, reading Parquet natively and speaking standard SQL with no dialect of its own. An external process opened against the same files reads the same bytes with the engine uninstalled.

clauses.subject: quiet-table
clauses.statement: The relation a quiet table registers as is {{store.declare.invariant.empty-table-is-a-zero-row-relation}} A caller reading it receives an empty result instead of a missing-relation fault.

clauses.subject: bare-name
clauses.statement: A bare table name in any read — a caller statement, a template body, a ranking arm, a file preview — resolves to that caller's registered relation. Restriction lives in the relation rather than in a clause each surface has to remember, which is what makes a later arm safe to add.

clauses.subject: tool-set
clauses.statement: The read face exposes a closed set: `context.describe` for what is queryable, `context.query` as the one call crossing structured and semantic retrieval, `context.execute_query` for pre-approved templates, `context.files` and `context.file` over committed data files, and `corpus.retrieve` for ranked reads across a prefix. A caller restricted to templates emits no SQL at all.

clauses.subject: describe-payload
clauses.statement: `context.describe` answers with the row count, the stored schema fingerprint over injected and declared columns, a table-level description, per-column hints, the declared index inventory, the partition scheme, `limits.max_rows`, the zone label, the store's lexicon, and worked example queries — enough to write a working query with no round trip.

clauses.subject: advertised-is-enforced
clauses.statement: A bound appears in a table's published `limits` block exactly when the engine applies it. An unenforceable bound is absent from the block rather than advertised, so a published number and a delivered guarantee cannot disagree.

clauses.subject: template-projection
clauses.statement: Every manifest template projects into a tool: the template identifier becomes the tool name and its declared positional parameters become a typed schema whose fields are all required. Adding a metric is adding a template, with no deploy of the calling application.

clauses.subject: ungranted-template
clauses.statement: Tool listing is filtered by the caller's grants, and a template absent from that listing is also unreachable by a guessed identifier, raising `TemplateNotGranted`. A listing therefore discloses no identifier the caller cannot run.

clauses.subject: file-listing
clauses.statement: `context.files` answers with paths relative to the store root for the tables the caller reads, and a table outside that set contributes no path — a listing cannot reveal that a table exists.

clauses.subject: file-preview-target
clauses.statement: `context.file` resolves a path to its `(table, run_id)` pair and reads the rows back through that table's registered relation, so row restriction, masks and the zone gate apply to a preview identically. A snapshot part, a traversal, an absolute path and a ledger file resolve to no table and raise `FilePreviewNotATable`.

clauses.subject: ledger-relation
clauses.statement: Each table's per-run request ledger registers as the child relation `<table>__requests`, holding identifiers, connector, method, host, status and timing for mediated outbound calls.

clauses.subject: scoped-ledger
clauses.statement: The child relation registers on the owner read alone — no grant allowlist, no row predicate, no column mask, no tenant scope. A tenant-scoped token naming it raises `LedgerNotTenantScoped` stating what closed the relation, rather than an empty result reading as no vendor traffic.

clauses.subject: lexicon-surface
clauses.statement: A store's declared lexicon reaches a caller through the describe payload. Numeric-identifier and badge vocabulary crosses to a rendering client; aliases, time-window phrases and distillation examples stay on the serving side, where interpretation happens.

clauses.subject: reserved-relation
clauses.statement: The engine's own reserved table namespaces register like any other relation and carry no privileged path underneath: a surface reading them reads through the same registration a caller gets.

clauses.subject: single-read-only-statement
clauses.statement: Admitted text parses to exactly one read-only SELECT. Attach, copy, install, load, pragma, set, every schema change and every data modification, and a piggybacked second statement all raise `StatementNotReadOnly`.

clauses.subject: engine-own-parse
clauses.statement: The guard walks the abstract syntax tree the engine itself executes, obtained by asking the engine to serialize the statement, so guard and executor cannot disagree about what a text means. Queries alone serialize; read-only-ness is a property of that representation rather than a blocklist someone maintains.

clauses.subject: relation-allowlist
clauses.statement: The decisive half is the relation-name allowlist: every base relation names either a view registered for this caller or a common table expression the statement itself declares. A bare path is an ordinary base relation at parse time and becomes a file read at bind time, so rejecting table-function nodes alone sails past it.

clauses.subject: whole-tree-walk
clauses.statement: The walk covers the entire tree — a scalar subquery inside the select list, a union arm, a pivot source — and gathers common-table-expression names across the tree before checking any base relation, as a relation may reference a name an ancestor node bound.

clauses.subject: unregistered-relation
clauses.statement: A base relation naming nothing this connection registered raises `RelationNotRegistered`. The message names what the statement asked for and echoes no relation belonging to another caller.

clauses.subject: table-function
clauses.statement: A table function anywhere in the tree, and a schema-qualified reach into a system catalog, raise `TableFunctionRefused`.

clauses.subject: statement-provenance
clauses.statement: Admission binds on who authored the text, not on how privileged the caller is. Operator-authored text — the local command line, a template body whose caller supplies an identifier and typed arguments, and reads the engine composes for itself — executes raw with table functions available; text a capability-token caller wrote is gated. The raw surface is reachable from nowhere on the network.

clauses.subject: quoted-identifiers
clauses.statement: Every schema- or manifest-derived identifier is double-quoted where it is rendered. A connector copies each vendor key into a column name verbatim, and an unquoted name parses as an expression and executes ungated. Quoting is not a character rule: a quoted identifier expresses any UTF-8 name, so a legitimate vendor field is admitted however it is spelled.

clauses.subject: template-declaration
clauses.statement: A template declares an identifier, one SQL statement, positional typed parameters written `name:type` over integer, float, string, timestamp and boolean, and an optional row ceiling.

clauses.subject: template-relation-shape
clauses.statement: Manifest validation and face startup refuse a template whose SQL names anything but the store's own tables as plain identifiers, raising `TemplateNamesForeignRelation`. A plain identifier carries a path separator where a prefixed table name needs one, and carries no dot, no star and no leading separator.

clauses.subject: template-binding
clauses.statement: Argument binding is strict: a missing, unknown or type-mismatched value raises `TemplateArgumentRejected` ahead of any execution, with no silent coercion. Placeholders cover exactly the declared parameters, and an identifier colliding with a built-in tool prefix is refused at the same two points.

clauses.subject: startup-time-check
clauses.statement: Template checks are caller-independent and run once at startup, so a reviewer who approves a template approves what it reads and a request pays nothing for the check.

clauses.subject: subject-values-are-parameters
clauses.statement: Values describing the caller reach a statement through parameter slots joined against a session-scoped relation. A principal value containing SQL syntax stays inert, as a parameter slot cannot become syntax.

clauses.subject: one-projection
clauses.statement: The command line's JSON output, the HTTP face and the tool protocol serialize one canonical projection: `columns`, `rows`, `truncated`, and the optional restriction, resolved-build, provenance, retrieval and time-bound blocks. A guarantee cannot land on one transport and be omitted by another.

clauses.subject: row-ceiling
clauses.statement: A per-table row ceiling published as `limits.max_rows` bounds a result, applied at execution with an over-fetch of 1 rows. The ceiling bounds rows delivered rather than work performed, so a bounded read over an expensive join still performs the join.

clauses.subject: truncation-is-exact
clauses.statement: `truncated` is set by the presence of the over-fetched probe row, which proves rows exist past the ceiling. It is mandatory and never derived by comparing a returned count against a requested limit, so a deliberately sized read and a capped one stay distinguishable.

clauses.subject: cell-encoding
clauses.statement: A cell carries its SQL value exactly. SQL NULL is JSON `null` and nothing else is; booleans are `true` and `false`; integers within ±(2^53−1) are numbers and wider ones exact decimal strings; finite floats are numbers and non-finite ones `"NaN"`, `"inf"` and `"-inf"`; decimals of 15 digits or fewer are numbers and wider ones exact text; dates, times and timestamps are ISO-8601 strings; intervals are ISO-8601 durations; binary is `\xAA`-form hex; an enum is its label; a container renders as its text form.

clauses.subject: wide-number-shape
clauses.statement: Whether an integer column serializes as JSON numbers or as strings is decided once for the whole column from the values one response carries, never cell by cell. The guarantee's scope is that single response, so two pages of one statement can disagree, and a caller wanting a value-independent wire shape casts the column to text in its query.

clauses.subject: type-is-the-cell
clauses.statement: No separate type list rides the envelope: a cell's JSON type is the declaration. A second, independently derived list contradicts it wherever the engine reports two distinct renderings under one physical type.

clauses.subject: zero-rows-is-success
clauses.statement: Returning fewer rows than the requested limit, zero included, is a success rather than an error. That is what lets a caller say the store holds nothing on a subject instead of serving unrelated rows.

clauses.subject: match-count
clauses.statement: Match counts ride outside any internals opt-in, so a caller learns how many rows the ranker scored as matching without asking for engine detail and without a second call.

clauses.subject: coverage-is-a-count
clauses.statement: A claim that the corpus lacks coverage of a subject comes from a count over the table with no recency truncation, taken after the full-scan fallback. A ranked result's top score cannot serve it: min-max normalization pins the best row at 1.0, and inverse-document-frequency weighting lifts a single incidental mention of a rare term.

clauses.subject: internals-opt-in
clauses.statement: Executed SQL, the engine name, the applied limit, the row count and elapsed milliseconds ride a separate object returned when a call sets `internals: true`. With the flag unset the response echoes none of them, and the split holds across every read tool and the HTTP face.

clauses.subject: operator-metadata
clauses.statement: Table metadata on the operator surface carries the column count and the backing file list; a description carries neither. A row count is an ordinary count query rather than a metadata field, as a maintained count is a second source of truth over one set of files.

clauses.subject: in-band-error
clauses.statement: On the tool protocol a refusal arrives in-band: a transport success carrying a protocol error object or a result flagged as an error. A caller judges an outcome by the result rather than by transport status.

clauses.subject: paths-stay-inside
clauses.statement: A result of an ordinary read carries no store path. Provenance is answered with columns naming table, run, connector version, ingestion instant and authoring subject, and where bytes sit is withheld deliberately.

clauses.subject: ranked-call
clauses.statement: `corpus.retrieve({prefix, query, kinds, limit, as_of})` answers with the top rows across the item and artifact genres under one prefix, each row carrying a snippet and full provenance. It composes the query surface and the memory recall path beneath itself and adds no storage of its own.

clauses.subject: relevance-floor
clauses.statement: A row reaches a caller when its lexical score is null, or is at least the floor, or its vector score exceeds zero. The floor is 2 for a content-token set of three or more members and 1 otherwise; a caller-supplied minimum overrides it, and a minimum of zero restores an unfiltered window.

clauses.subject: content-tokens
clauses.statement: The query text is lowercased and split on non-alphanumeric characters. Stop tokens drop, non-ASCII runs of two or more characters are kept, and what survives is deduplicated with its order preserved.

clauses.subject: token-length-floor
clauses.statement: An ASCII run shorter than 2 chars is discarded from the content-token set.

clauses.subject: token-cap
clauses.statement: The content-token set holds at most 12 tokens. An empty set omits the relevance predicate entirely, leaving a browse-shaped read unaffected.

clauses.subject: script-split-matching
clauses.statement: An all-lowercase-alphanumeric token matches on an ASCII word boundary with an optional plural suffix; a token carrying any non-ASCII character matches by containment. An ASCII word boundary cannot occur beside an ideograph, and a single anchoring rule for both scripts silently deletes rows that literally carry the term.

clauses.subject: plural-suffix-floor
clauses.statement: The optional plural suffix is dropped for a token under 4 chars, so a short term cannot match a longer unrelated word that merely starts with it.

clauses.subject: text-free-table-scores-null
clauses.statement: The lexical score is null rather than zero for a table carrying no snippet-worthy text column, so the floor cannot delete an entire table from a search; such a table's rows are admitted by the vector score alone.

clauses.subject: candidate-window
clauses.statement: The candidate window is 8 times the requested limit or 200 rows, whichever is larger. Candidates equal to the window report that the question's terms matched more rows than the window holds and the ranking saw a recency-ordered slice; a larger requested limit widens it. This is the one truncation a caller cannot otherwise detect.

clauses.subject: reserved-columns-project-null
clauses.statement: Reserved projected columns — modality, language, prompt hash, kind — render as null for a table that does not carry them, so a table missing one contributes its rows to the union instead of dropping out of the search.

clauses.subject: unsatisfiable-arm-drops
clauses.statement: `filter` binds caller-named columns. A table lacking a named column makes its arm unsatisfiable, and that arm is dropped rather than emitted unfiltered, so an equality predicate cannot come back with every row of a table that has no such column.

clauses.subject: engine-resolved-date
clauses.statement: The publication column is resolved by the engine per table rather than routed through the caller's filter, so a store spelling its date column differently keeps its rows inside time-framed handling instead of losing them to one name.

clauses.subject: filter-budget
clauses.statement: A filter carries at most 256 entries in a membership list, with its condition count and total byte size bounded alongside.

clauses.subject: filter-budget
clauses.statement: The budget is checked once over the whole filter ahead of building any arm, and an oversized or malformed condition raises `FilterBudgetExceeded` for the whole read rather than quietly dropping the table the condition appeared under.

clauses.subject: row-key-dedup
clauses.statement: A ranked read keeps one row per `(table, row key)`, newest ingestion first. The row key is the table's declared content-hash column and null otherwise — never a digest computed by concatenating projected values, as concatenation skips nulls and folds a text-free table into a single row.

clauses.subject: row-key-stays-internal
clauses.statement: The row key is absent from the outer projection, so a content hash never reaches a snippet or a rendered cell.

clauses.subject: dedup-is-gated
clauses.statement: The deduplicating window function is gated on the same condition as the relevance floor, as on a browse-shaped read it defeats top-N pushdown and costs measurable milliseconds for nothing.

clauses.subject: snippet
clauses.statement: A row's snippet is built from label-priority text columns — title, summary, description, thesis and their kin — then the remaining prose-worthy text columns in schema order, at most three, concatenated with a separator.

clauses.subject: identifiers-never-snippet
clauses.statement: Content hashes, URLs, identifiers and instant-valued columns never qualify for a snippet. Landed schemas are alphabetized, and without the exclusion the first text column becomes every snippet and blinds both the ranker and the reader.

clauses.subject: sidecar-generates-candidates
clauses.statement: The vector sidecar arm performs candidate generation rather than rescoring: it admits the recency window the exact scan considers plus the sidecar's own top results, and every candidate is re-scored through the caller's registration. Per-row scores are identical to the exact path; which rows enter the window is what changes.

clauses.subject: sidecar-oversampling
clauses.statement: One probe requests 4 times the requested limit or 64 rows, whichever is larger, multiplied by 4 where the request carries restriction context, so slots spent on rows a reader cannot see are compensated proportionally.

clauses.subject: sidecar-size-cap
clauses.statement: A sidecar holding more than 64 MiB of stored vectors is left unloaded and the arm takes the exact scan.

clauses.subject: sidecar-falls-back
clauses.statement: Every sidecar precondition failure falls back to the exact scan: no snapshot, no matching sidecar, a multi-column or masked key, a dimension or manifest mismatch, an unreadable dump, or mixed producers on one table. An identifier surviving in a sidecar after its row was purged resolves to no row through the registration and filters away.

clauses.subject: gain-never-loss
clauses.statement: The accelerated arm is a strict superset of the exact path for one reader: rows are gained, none is lost. Two readers issuing one query against one snapshot can nonetheless recall different rows, as the probe ranges over rows neither of them sees.

clauses.subject: three-legs
clauses.statement: Ranking runs three legs: exact cosine similarity over the candidate set, BM25 over a full-text index, and a weighted fusion of the two.

clauses.subject: fusion
clauses.statement: Fusion computes `w_vec · clamp(cosine, 0, 1) + w_lex · minmax(bm25)` with default weights of 0.6 for the vector leg and 0.4 for the lexical one. A document present in one leg contributes zero for the other, so fusion degrades into a single-signal ranking, and ties break by identifier for a deterministic order.

clauses.subject: lexical-leg-matches-only
clauses.statement: The BM25 leg ranks over a disjunction of should-clauses, so a document matching no query term is absent from the ranking rather than merely last. An empty query, an empty candidate set or a zero result count yields an empty ranking that falls back to recency ordering.

clauses.subject: flat-window-full-credit
clauses.statement: A lexical window whose scores carry no spread awards every present document full credit, leaving the fused order to the other leg and the tie-break.

clauses.subject: question-window-is-a-tier
clauses.statement: A question's timeframe projects a per-row in-window flag against the resolved publication column, and that flag leads the ordering. A row outside the timeframe sorts down and is never dropped, so a store with nothing fresh answers with its most recent picture instead of presenting old rows as current.

clauses.subject: window-anchor-tolerance
clauses.statement: A publication instant more than 24 h past the question's anchor resolves the in-window flag to false. A null date and unparseable text resolve it the same way, rather than raising an error or removing the row, and a basis field names which case applied.

clauses.subject: ordering-casts-first
clauses.statement: Ordering casts a publication value before comparing it, as a text comparison of two date spellings is a comparison of strings and not of instants.

clauses.subject: retrieval-block
clauses.statement: The retrieval block reports `window`, `candidates_prefloor`, `candidates`, `matched`, `returned`, `in_window`, `deduped`, `padded`, `floor` and `since`. Per row a caller receives an integer score bounded by the content-token count, a boolean in-window flag, and the basis label.

clauses.subject: internal-score-stays-internal
clauses.statement: The lexical engine's own float never crosses to a caller. It is corpus-relative, and a consumer thresholding on it drifts silently as the corpus changes underneath the number.

clauses.subject: absent-block
clauses.statement: The retrieval block is omitted from every statement that is not a ranked read, and from a build carrying no ranker, where no honest number exists to report. A consumer distinguishes an absent block from a present block reporting zero matches.

clauses.subject: degradation-not-error
clauses.statement: Without the lexical backend linked, ranking substitutes a token fallback that scores each query token over the snippet, with recency breaking ties and ordering the empty-query case. The result is a different order, not a failed call.

clauses.subject: fallback-counts-tokens
clauses.statement: Under the fallback every matching token contributes, so hyphenated, spaced and possessive phrasings of one phrase rank equivalently, and a row carrying terms outranks a row that is merely newer.

clauses.subject: caller-embedding
clauses.statement: Supplying a query embedding turns on per-row cosine and fuses it with the lexical leg; omitting one leaves every projected column identical to the lexical-only path. The vectors a caller supplies come from the model the stored rows record.

clauses.subject: lexical-index-cache
clauses.statement: The full-text index is keyed on a fingerprint over the candidate documents, which is query-independent while the window is recency-selected, and cached in a FIFO of 64 entries. A changed snapshot, table set or time bound changes the fingerprint, so a stale index cannot serve a changed corpus.

clauses.subject: statistics-over-the-widened-window
clauses.statement: Lexical term statistics are computed over the widened candidate window, so an accelerated arm can order rows differently from the exact path even where the per-row scores agree exactly.

clauses.subject: transports-are-byte-identical
clauses.statement: The two calls exposing ranked retrieval assemble identical response bodies and change together. A guarantee reaching one of them and missing the other is worse than one reaching neither.

clauses.subject: hot-local-parquet
clauses.statement: The retrieval container syncs the current snapshot set to local disk and memory-maps it. Object storage is the durable source and stays out of the per-query path, and clustering zone maps prune the scan to the relevant row groups.

clauses.subject: cold-start
clauses.statement: A cold retrieval container reaches readiness within 8 s, and a container holding no snapshot pays a whole-store pull on top of that before its first answer.

clauses.subject: result-key
clauses.statement: A result cache keys on the full policy subject — the token's scope, the inference zone, and incognito state — combined with the hash of the statement, so a hit cannot cross a restriction boundary.

clauses.subject: cache-is-opt-in
clauses.statement: The result cache is opt-in per table at a short time to live, and off for a table tagged private. A deployment that enables nothing caches nothing.

clauses.subject: snapshot-invalidates
clauses.statement: A newly committed snapshot invalidates every cached entry keyed against the tables it folds, and an entry keyed against a superseded snapshot serves no later read. What a statement already in flight during a fold reads is {{store.fold.invariant.reads-are-non-blocking}}

clauses.subject: keep-warm-is-per-deployment
clauses.statement: A deployment carrying active traffic keeps its retrieval container warm. Sub-second latency is a property of the warm path, and a deployment that declines keep-warm accepts a cold first read in exchange for no cost at rest.

clauses.subject: pin-parameter
clauses.statement: `pin` maps a table name to a build identifier and resolves each named table to the state that build published and to no other. An unnamed table resolves to the latest published state.

clauses.subject: unknown-build
clauses.statement: An unknown or collected build identifier raises `PinnedBuildUnavailable`, naming the oldest identifier still pinnable. A pin is never quietly widened to the latest state.

clauses.subject: earlier-bound-wins
clauses.statement: A pin and the store's transaction-time bound are both upper bounds on one clock, and a table named by both resolves to whichever of the two is earlier.

clauses.subject: resolved-echo
clauses.statement: A response touching a published model carries `contextful.resolved`, mapping each such table to its `{build_id, watermark}`, whether or not the request passed a pin. A consumer records which state produced the rows it writes.

clauses.subject: absent-watermark
clauses.statement: The watermark is null for a materialization that carries none, and its absence is distinct from a watermark of zero.

clauses.subject: consumer-comparison
clauses.statement: The check the echo exists for: a consumer compares resolved build identifiers across every query of one derivation and fails that derivation where two differ, rather than writing rows stitched from two states.

clauses.subject: client-packaging
clauses.statement: Putting search and an ask experience inside a third-party page is client packaging rather than an engine extension: the engine stays a service a caller talks to, and the kit is a thin layer over the tool protocol and query contract the container already serves.

clauses.subject: headless-client
clauses.statement: The library is a headless, zero-dependency, zero-build ES module over a transport, exposing `search()`, `query()`, `tables()`, `describe()`, `retrieve()`, `recall()`, `remember()`, `predict()` and `ask()`.

clauses.subject: one-call-per-read
clauses.statement: Every read is one tool call, so one body of code runs unchanged on every transport — a browser, a server runtime, an edge isolate.

clauses.subject: search-tool
clauses.statement: The free-text search tool takes `{query, query_embedding?, tables?, limit}` and reuses the ranked path underneath. Omitting the embedding preserves the lexical-only behavior; supplying one fuses cosine similarity into the ordering.

clauses.subject: four-shapes
clauses.statement: Four deployment shapes share the one client: a host backend proxying same-origin and injecting the token server-side; a host backend on the same account collapsing that hop into a service binding; an engine-direct browser embed holding a scoped token itself; and a local consumer spawning the engine as a child process over newline-framed JSON-RPC with no listener and no issuer key.

clauses.subject: typed-entrypoint
clauses.statement: The gateway exports a typed entrypoint with `query(sql)`, `mcp(message)` and `health()`, bound account-internally by a host backend. The binding is the perimeter, with no public hop, and the entrypoint injects the container-side credential so the host holds no secret.

clauses.subject: per-request-token
clauses.statement: A per-request capability token runs the read under that token's own grants inside the engine, identically to the HTTP face. A transport changes who injects the credential and never what the credential is worth.

clauses.subject: wildcard-origin
clauses.statement: Cross-origin access is off by default and opt-in. Authentication is a bearer header and never a cookie, so a wildcard origin is non-credentialed, which is what lets the face be embedded in an application with no backend at all.

clauses.subject: per-viewer-token
clauses.statement: A browser-held credential is minted per viewer: the host exchanges the visitor's verified assertion at the engine's exchange route for a least-privilege token audience-bound to one store, scoped and audited under that identity. It expires in minutes and is verified at both hops over the same transmitted bytes, and absent holder binding a leaked token is replayable for its remaining lifetime.

clauses.subject: build-identity
clauses.statement: The handshake reports what a binary linked under one rule with no per-face argument: retrieval backends `duckdb`, `fts` and `hnsw`; connector families `m365`, `s3` and `wasm`; and the binary's own faces `http`, `eval` and `otlp`. The set composes by asking each crate declaring those features, and the same composition backs the version output, so the two faces cannot disagree about one binary.

clauses.subject: required-face
clauses.statement: A client passing `require: [...]` has each name matched against the reported set and is refused ahead of its first read with `RequiredFaceAbsent`; an engine reporting no set satisfies no requirement. Reporting is itself never a refusal, as most absences are degradations the engine serves through.

clauses.subject: two-absence-shapes
clauses.statement: Two absences are distinguishable at the call. Without the lexical backend, retrieval swaps BM25 for the token fallback — a different ranking. Without the vector backend, a supplied embedding still scores, over the rows the recency window already recalled, as the approximate arm contributes no candidates.

clauses.subject: absent-read-backend
clauses.statement: Without the embedded SQL engine linked, both read tools refuse outright with `ReadBackendAbsent` rather than answering from a narrower path.

clauses.subject: ask-event-stream
clauses.statement: The ask experience streams typed events from a backend running the model: `tool`, `tool_result`, `text`, `citations`, `notice`, `console.render`, `done` and `error`. The citations event follows the answer text and carries the numbered sources — title, link, publication day, and whether a source is data or web. The model lives outside the engine, so the engine-direct shape serves no ask and its client points at a separate streaming endpoint.

clauses.subject: stdio-credential
clauses.statement: Over the process transport a credential is mandatory — a capability token string, or an explicit owner flag. An unset token resolves to the owner context, which is the ungated branch for every tool including run execution and memory writes, so the client raises `StdioCredentialMissing` rather than escalating in silence.

clauses.subject: child-environment
clauses.statement: An explicit passthrough list is all that crosses into the spawned engine, defaulting to the executable search path and the home directory. The engine's secret resolver reads vendor credentials straight out of its environment, and an inherited environment hands a child every key its parent holds.

clauses.subject: store-selector
clauses.statement: The child's working directory selects the store: the process walks up for the project manifest and, finding none, raises `StoreSelectorAbsent` and exits ahead of writing one byte of protocol framing. The executable path and the working directory are trusted inputs, executed and read as given.

clauses.subject: serial-dispatch
clauses.statement: The process transport keeps exactly one request in flight: the engine reads a line, answers it, and only then reads the next, so an aborted call resynchronizes by discarding exactly one reply.

clauses.subject: process-subpath
clauses.statement: The process transport lives on its own import subpath, so a child-process import never reaches the root entry an isolate bundles.

clauses.subject: memory-shape
clauses.statement: Synthesized memory is five table shapes over one substrate: `memory_episodes` holds one row per session window, `memory_facts` one row per durable claim, `memory_entities` one row per resolved thing, `memory_edges` one row per directed relationship, `memory_preferences` one row per subject-key pair.

clauses.subject: shape-declaration
clauses.statement: A table names `shape` beside its columns. The declaration binds the schema validator to that shape's canonical column set and tells the tool surface which ranking defaults to publish.

clauses.subject: canonical-column
clauses.statement: A table naming a shape and omitting a canonical column of that shape raises `MemoryShapeColumnMissing` when the declaration loads.

clauses.subject: fact-columns
clauses.statement: `memory_facts` carries `fact_id`, `subject_id`, `predicate`, `object`, `confidence`, `scope`, `tier`, `support`, `evidence_row_ids`, `prompt_version`, `dedup_key`, `superseded_by`, and the declared validity pair.

clauses.subject: entity-columns
clauses.statement: `memory_entities` carries `entity_id`, a display name, per-language aliases, an attribute map, and a last-seen instant.

clauses.subject: edge-columns
clauses.statement: `memory_edges` carries `src_id`, `dst_id`, `rel_type`, `weight`, the validity pair, and the provenance columns a claim row carries.

clauses.subject: episode-columns
clauses.statement: `memory_episodes` carries an episode id, the window start and end it covers, a summary, the set of source tables it read, and the evidence row identifiers folded into that summary.

clauses.subject: preference-columns
clauses.statement: `memory_preferences` carries `subject_id`, `key`, `value`, `confidence` and `scope`, holding one live row per subject-key pair under the revision rule a claim follows.

clauses.subject: validity-pair
clauses.statement: A memory shape names its validity columns through the same table declaration any other table uses, so live recall and a validity-bounded read resolve one column pair rather than two independent ones.

clauses.subject: tier
clauses.statement: `tier` takes `curated` for a human or a version-controlled file a human wrote, `derived` for synthesis over rows from a source the deployment declared, and `researched` for synthesis over rows the system fetched on its own initiative.

clauses.subject: scope
clauses.statement: `scope` is an optional string stamped when a row is synthesized or asserted, partitioning one subject's claims across the surfaces that produced them.

clauses.subject: relation-type
clauses.statement: The relation vocabulary is a reserved core — `same_as`, `part_of`, `member_of`, `located_in`, `derived_from`, `precedes`, `causes`, `mentions` — unioned with the types one deployment declares. The set is closed within that deployment, so a filter on `rel_type` reads reliably.

clauses.subject: undeclared-relation
clauses.statement: A candidate edge whose `rel_type` falls outside that union lands in the dead-letter table and raises `MemoryUndeclaredRelation`, and no row is written under the unknown type.

clauses.subject: relation-flags
clauses.statement: A declared relation type carries optional inverse and symmetric flags, read by traversal as hints over materialized rows and by nothing that infers a row.

clauses.subject: place-tables
clauses.statement: The place dimension, its per-language aliases, and the map from a place to the entities exposed at it are three tables the deployment supplies as CSV.

clauses.subject: extract-template
clauses.statement: The deployment supplies the extract template and the output schema every candidate validates against. The engine supplies the matcher, the deduplication key, the revision rule and the tier derivation.

clauses.subject: synthesis-stage
clauses.statement: Synthesis runs Extract, then Resolve, then Consolidate. Extract reads rows landed since the pass's last cursor and emits candidates; Resolve is deterministic; Consolidate deduplicates and writes.

clauses.subject: extract
clauses.statement: Extract is the one stage that calls a model. It emits `(subject, predicate, object, confidence, evidence_row_ids)` tuples, entity mentions and candidate edges, each validated against the declared output schema.

clauses.subject: candidate-schema
clauses.statement: A candidate failing the declared output schema is fed back for one further attempt and raises `MemoryCandidateSchemaInvalid` on the terminal attempt. No free-text path converts an unvalidated response into a row.

clauses.subject: extract-attempts
clauses.statement: Extract retries a schema-invalid response with feedback at most 3 attempts per batch.

clauses.subject: dead-letter
clauses.statement: A batch exhausting its attempts writes the response, the template hash and the drop reason to the dead-letter table and raises `MemoryExtractExhausted`, leaving the cursor unadvanced for that batch.

clauses.subject: dedup-key
clauses.statement: Each candidate carries `dedup_key = sha256(prompt_hash ‖ source_row_ids ‖ canonical_subject ‖ predicate)`.

clauses.subject: idempotence
clauses.statement: Consolidate upserts on `dedup_key`, so repeating a pass over the same rows under the same template writes nothing new.

clauses.subject: prompt-version
clauses.statement: Re-extracting one row set under a changed template yields a different key. Both generations coexist, told apart by `prompt_version`, and a rewrite command retires the earlier generation under a drop-or-merge strategy the caller names.

clauses.subject: template-hash
clauses.statement: The prompt hash covers the operator's template alone. The data markers wrapping ingested values sit outside the identity contract, so hardening that boundary leaves every existing key intact.

clauses.subject: support
clauses.statement: Every claim carries `support = {contributors, records}` stamped from pre-aggregation counts: `records` is the evidence row count, `contributors` is the count of distinct contributor keys the ingesting pipeline declares per source row, falling back to distinct source tables and then to 1.

clauses.subject: support-is-derived
clauses.statement: `support` is computed at write time and takes no part in `dedup_key`, so a replay whose attribution shifted remains a no-op on the row it already wrote.

clauses.subject: support-band
clauses.statement: Under a banded reporting setting `support` renders as `0`, `1-9`, `10-99` or `100+` in place of a count.

clauses.subject: contributor-key
clauses.statement: A fetched result stamps its contributor key as the result's registrable domain, so `contributors` counts distinct publishers rather than distinct retrievals of one publisher.

clauses.subject: tier-derivation
clauses.statement: `tier` is computed when the row is written, from the writing grant and the run's source, and is read from no field of the write payload. A pass whose grounding mixed declared-source rows with a self-directed fetch takes the lowest tier across its legs.

clauses.subject: audit-record
clauses.statement: Each stage emits the run's standard spans plus the endpoint, the model id, the template hash, input and output token counts, the candidate drop reason, the entity action — merged, created, or ambiguous skip — and the claim action — inserted, superseded, decayed, or duplicate skip.

clauses.subject: lineage
clauses.statement: Every memory row resolves back to the pass that produced it, the model that produced it, and the source rows it was distilled from, through columns the row carries rather than an external log.

clauses.subject: commit
clauses.statement: A memory write runs the post-run commit the write path uses, so the rows and the catalog that serves recall survive a restart and are restored by a cold-start pull.

clauses.subject: coverage-gap
clauses.statement: A coverage gap on a subject closes when a declared source covers that subject. An answer assembled from a self-directed fetch is a stopgap and leaves the gap open.

clauses.subject: gap-record
clauses.statement: An open gap records the subject, the gap kind, the pass that observed it, and the instant it was last observed open.

clauses.subject: supersession
clauses.statement: A landing claim retires the prior live claim on the same `(subject_id, predicate, scope)`. The retired row takes `superseded_by` set to the landing claim's `fact_id` and its validity end set to the landing claim's validity start.

clauses.subject: retired-row-stays
clauses.statement: A retired row remains in the table for audit and for a point-in-time read, and falls out of live serving through the liveness predicate every consumer already applies.

clauses.subject: confidence-decay
clauses.statement: Retirement multiplies the retired row's `confidence` by 0.5 when the object changed. A reaffirmation carrying the same object leaves the retired confidence untouched.

clauses.subject: validity-line
clauses.statement: Two claims revise each other when both carry an open validity end, or when both are anchored to the same validity start. A past-anchored belief and a present belief about one subject and predicate coexist on separate lines.

clauses.subject: replay-skips-revision
clauses.statement: A candidate arriving under a `dedup_key` already present resolves as an upsert and reaches the revision rule not at all.

clauses.subject: batch-collision
clauses.statement: Two claims about one subject and predicate landing inside a single batch are both kept, and the revision rule runs against rows already committed rather than against siblings of the same batch.

clauses.subject: tier-precedence
clauses.statement: A claim retires a prior of equal or higher standing. A claim of lower standing that contradicts a live higher-standing claim lands with a bounded validity end and never live, leaving one live belief per subject, predicate and scope.

clauses.subject: direct-write
clauses.statement: The direct write accepts claims. It declines the other four shapes and names the entity upsert as the door for an entity row.

clauses.subject: direct-write-shape
clauses.statement: A direct write naming `memory_episodes`, `memory_entities`, `memory_edges` or `memory_preferences` raises `MemoryDirectWriteShapeRefused`.

clauses.subject: anchor
clauses.statement: An `observed_at` anchor sets the claim's validity start and validity end to that instant, a point interval, while the ingestion clock stamps the present.

clauses.subject: anchor-outside-identity
clauses.statement: An anchor stays outside the identity hash, so a caller varying the vantage varies the claim's evidence qualification to keep two anchored assertions apart.

clauses.subject: assertion-provenance
clauses.statement: A direct write records its stage as a direct assertion and stamps the author's subject tuple, so an asserted claim and a synthesized claim are told apart in the audit record.

clauses.subject: assertion-citation
clauses.statement: A direct assertion's textual citations are governed by the claim table's own read rules, and are not resolved as evidence row references.

clauses.subject: expiry
clauses.statement: A `researched` claim carries an expiry. A scheduled pass stamps a validity end on an expired claim that no promotion covered, and the row itself stays in place.

clauses.subject: retention
clauses.statement: An expired `researched` claim survives when an artifact's provenance cites it or a human promotes it. Retention reads citation rather than reads, and a `curated` or `derived` claim carries no expiry.

clauses.subject: promotion
clauses.statement: Promotion to a higher tier patches the record and appends a marker pass in the shape supersession uses. The synthesizing agent stays recorded and the promoting human is stamped beside it.

clauses.subject: edge-revision
clauses.statement: An edge row follows the claim revision rule over `(src_id, rel_type, dst_id, scope)`, carrying the same validity-line scoping and the same retirement stamps.

clauses.subject: present-time
clauses.statement: Recall answers as of now and accepts no time bound of its own. A reader asking what the workspace believed on an earlier day issues a bounded read over the claim mirror instead.

clauses.subject: recall-clocks
clauses.statement: Recall bounds two clocks that answer different questions: the session's vantage bounds when a row entered the store, and the validity columns bound what the row claims to hold true of.

clauses.subject: open-interval
clauses.statement: A present-time read returns open-ended intervals. A read at a vantage of one day additionally returns the point intervals anchored to that day.

clauses.subject: fold
clauses.statement: Recall keeps the latest row per `dedup_key`, and drops a tombstoned row and a superseded row before ranking.

clauses.subject: tier-order
clauses.statement: Recall orders by `tier` first and by score second, so standing decides ahead of magnitude.

clauses.subject: score
clauses.statement: Within one tier the score multiplies `confidence` by a rank-position factor of `(index + 1) / total` over the live claim set.

clauses.subject: scope-filter
clauses.statement: A recall carrying a scope filter returns claims stamped with that exact scope and excludes unscoped claims. A recall carrying no filter returns every scope.

clauses.subject: evidence-gate
clauses.statement: A synthesized claim is served when every one of its evidence rows resolves and reads through the same enforced session the caller holds.

clauses.subject: evidence
clauses.statement: An evidence reference names a table carrying a declared single-column primary key or an `id` column, and the row identifier within it.

clauses.subject: evidence-unresolved
clauses.statement: An unreadable source row, a masked source row, an unknown table, a reference into another memory row, and malformed lineage each suppress the claim and raise `MemoryEvidenceUnresolved`.

clauses.subject: evidence-references
clauses.statement: A claim naming more than 256 entries of evidence is suppressed rather than resolved, raising `MemoryEvidenceOverflow`.

clauses.subject: zone-check
clauses.statement: Recall checks each row's inference zone against the zone the caller asserts, by the same rule a table read applies, rather than by a second check written for memory.

clauses.subject: only-door
clauses.statement: Memory tables are excluded from candidate generation on the read path, so a claim reaches an answer through recall rather than through a text match over the claim table.

clauses.subject: empty-store
clauses.statement: A store holding no claim table recalls a clean zero, and reports that as an answered read rather than an error.

clauses.subject: injection
clauses.statement: Recalled claims enter a grounded turn as an explicit block, carrying the instruction to state whether the turn's data confirms or contradicts each one, and the recall step itself is a visible trace step.

clauses.subject: knowledge-card-link
clauses.statement: A recall result carries each claim's `fact_id`, `tier`, `support` and evidence identifiers, so a reader reaches the card for its subject and the rows underneath it from the result alone.

clauses.subject: forget-call
clauses.statement: `memory.forget(shape, selector, reason, cascade)` names the shape to act on, the selector picking rows within it, a reason recorded on the marker, and whether the cascade runs.

clauses.subject: tombstone
clauses.statement: A forget writes a tombstone row visible to the audit trail, carrying the selector, its stated reason and the acting subject tuple.

clauses.subject: physical-delete
clauses.statement: The rows a tombstone covers leave the files at the next compaction, and the tombstone is what removes them from every read in between.

clauses.subject: cascade
clauses.statement: The cascade drops the synthesized rows whose evidence includes the forgotten subject, one hop out from the tombstoned rows.

clauses.subject: dry-run
clauses.statement: A dry run returns the cascade list and writes nothing, so the set a live call removes is reviewable ahead of the call.

clauses.subject: privilege
clauses.statement: Forget is excluded from the default grant set, and a caller holding a write grant without the forget grant raises `MemoryForgetUngranted`.

clauses.subject: marker-commit
clauses.statement: A tombstone and its cascade markers reach the bucket in the same commit as the rows they retire, so a replica's next pull sees the erasure rather than the rows.

clauses.subject: serving
clauses.statement: A tombstoned row is dropped ahead of ranking, and a cascade-marked row is dropped with it, so neither reaches a recall result or a knowledge card.

clauses.subject: resolve
clauses.statement: Resolve matches candidate mentions against `memory_entities` by alias, by embedding similarity and by deterministic keys, settling on a canonical `entity_id` or staging a new one, then tags each candidate claim with its resolved subject.

clauses.subject: entity-id
clauses.statement: `entity_id` is opaque: it carries no name, no ticker and no language, and a display change rewrites no identifier and no row that points at one.

clauses.subject: alias-normalization
clauses.statement: Per-language aliases normalize so script variants and full-width forms of one name fold onto a single identity. The engine owns the matcher; the deployment owns the alias sets it folds.

clauses.subject: alias-match-mode
clauses.statement: An alias carrying ideographic characters matches by containment. A latin or numeric alias matches on an ASCII word boundary at both ends, so `Electron` misses `electronics`.

clauses.subject: alias-stem
clauses.statement: A trailing `*` marks a prefix stem, holding the left boundary and dropping the right. `\*` is a literal asterisk. A stem on an ideographic alias changes nothing, and a stem widens tagging alone, staying out of the resolver's containment fallback.

clauses.subject: ambiguous-mention
clauses.statement: A mention matching two canonical identities with no deterministic key to separate them is recorded as an ambiguous skip, raising `MemoryEntityAmbiguous`, and the candidate claim carrying it is dead-lettered.

clauses.subject: knowledge-card
clauses.statement: `entity.explain(reference)` resolves a ticker, a name or an alias in any script to one authorized identity and returns its canonical id, display name, per-language aliases, attributes, last-seen instant, and the authorized claims about it.

clauses.subject: card-authorization
clauses.statement: The card requires a read grant on the entity table. Without a separate grant on claims the card returns its identity and no claims.

clauses.subject: entity-upsert
clauses.statement: The companion upsert writes one entity row, and the same writer is reachable from the command line, so a pipeline seeds identities without opening a tool session against the engine it runs inside.

clauses.subject: place-id
clauses.statement: A row answers which place it concerns through an opaque `place_id` stamped by the same matcher `entity_id` is stamped by.

clauses.subject: parent-closure
clauses.statement: Nearness is the transitive closure over the deployment's declared parent edges: near a place means at that place or under it. The closure is materialized once and joined as an ordinary dimension.

clauses.subject: no-geometry
clauses.statement: The engine holds no geometry type, no distance function and no radius. A spatial question is answered by the parent closure or not at all.

clauses.subject: place-left-join
clauses.statement: The join from a row onto the place alias dimension is a left join, so an unmapped place lands a null tag and the row survives for both the reader and the dimension's maintainer.

clauses.subject: place-fold
clauses.statement: Place resolution reads the latest row per key, so a re-landed snapshot source produces one tag per row rather than one per pull.

clauses.subject: edge-materialization
clauses.statement: An edge is an explicit typed row written when synthesis resolves both endpoints, and no edge is inferred while a query runs.

clauses.subject: edge-endpoint
clauses.statement: A candidate edge whose source or target resolves to no identity is dead-lettered and raises `MemoryEdgeEndpointUnresolved`.

clauses.subject: traversal
clauses.statement: Multi-hop traversal is a recursive query over `memory_edges`, seeded by resolution and by ranked recall, in the query language the read path already serves — no second language and no second consistency boundary.

clauses.subject: edge-provenance
clauses.statement: An edge row is stamped with lineage and validity in the same shape a claim is, so a traversal at a vantage sees the graph as it stood and cites its rows the same way.

clauses.subject: prediction
clauses.statement: `predictions` holds one row per emitted claim about the future: subject, target, the resolution form, the resolution key, the declared resolution source, `predicted_at`, and the confidence attached.

clauses.subject: observation
clauses.statement: `outcomes` holds one row per observed result: the prediction it settles, the verdict, the signal, the resolution source that produced it, the settling citation, and the instant observed.

clauses.subject: no-new-primitive
clauses.statement: Both tables sit on the store substrate and the label is a view over them, so settling introduces no storage engine, no scheduler and no runtime primitive of its own.

clauses.subject: resolution-form
clauses.statement: A registration names exactly one of a relative horizon, an absolute deadline, or an open-ended watch. Naming none and naming two both raise `OutcomeResolutionFormInvalid`.

clauses.subject: deadline-canonicalization
clauses.statement: A deadline given as a calendar day canonicalizes to midnight UTC on that day.

clauses.subject: scheduling
clauses.statement: An observation is scheduled asynchronously at the resolve instant. An open-ended watch is scheduled not at all and settles when something observes it.

clauses.subject: prediction-id
clauses.statement: A prediction id hashes `(subject, target, resolution key, predicted_at)`, with `predicted_at` defaulting to the present instant, so a bare re-emit writes a new row and an explicitly anchored re-emit collapses onto the first.

clauses.subject: observation-id
clauses.statement: An observation id hashes every field the row asserts, including verdict, source and citation. A byte-identical re-observation writes nothing, and two observations settling one prediction differently both land.

clauses.subject: resolution-source
clauses.statement: A registration declares `metric` — a comparator over an ingested observable — `adjudicator` — a resolver pass fed raw source rows — or `manual`, a human queue.

clauses.subject: comparator-custody
clauses.statement: A metric comparator is stored verbatim and evaluated outside the engine. The engine runs no expression language over a stored rule.

clauses.subject: unknown-source
clauses.statement: A registration naming a resolution source outside that set raises `OutcomeSourceUnknown` at parse and is stored not at all.

clauses.subject: comparator-missing
clauses.statement: A `metric` registration carrying no comparator raises `OutcomeComparatorMissing`.

clauses.subject: comparator-on-judgment
clauses.statement: A comparator supplied alongside `adjudicator` or `manual` raises `OutcomeComparatorOnJudgment`.

clauses.subject: unsourced-verdict
clauses.statement: An observation carrying a verdict and no resolution source raises `OutcomeVerdictUnsourced`.

clauses.subject: source-mismatch
clauses.statement: An observation whose resolution source contradicts the registration's raises `OutcomeSourceMismatch`, so a claim registered under a source owing a citation is settled under that source and no other.

clauses.subject: settling-citation
clauses.statement: A verdict from `adjudicator` or `manual` carries an `http` or `https` settling citation. Its absence raises `OutcomeCitationMissing`, and the citation rides the label view rather than the base table alone.

clauses.subject: undeclared-rule
clauses.statement: A verdict against a prediction that declared no resolution source is coerced to a null verdict under an undeclared-rule signal, however well it is cited.

clauses.subject: self-rated
clauses.statement: An outcome derived from the store's own rating carries a null verdict under a self-rated signal, stays visible for audit, and is excluded from every calibration figure. The exclusion lives in the view, since the outcomes table is writable by any pipeline.

clauses.subject: unresolved-signal
clauses.statement: An application supplies an `unresolved:<reason>` signal when its evidence cannot carry a verdict, and the engine holds the verdict null for every such signal.

clauses.subject: application-cadence
clauses.statement: Freshness thresholds and observation cadence belong to the application. The engine prescribes no rating schema, no domain judgment, and no interval between observations.

clauses.subject: outcome-label
clauses.statement: `outcome_labels` joins `predictions` to `outcomes` on prediction id and derives lead time in seconds between the prediction instant and the observation instant.

clauses.subject: grace-window
clauses.statement: The join keeps an observation from the prediction instant through the deadline plus an inclusive grace of 86400 s, so a settlement landing at or just after the deadline is scored rather than dropped.

clauses.subject: epoch-comparison
clauses.statement: Instants are stored as text, and the view casts them to epoch seconds before comparing, so the join runs over the same corpus on any SQL engine.

clauses.subject: view-partition
clauses.statement: `outcome_labels_unresolved` negates the scored predicate verbatim, and every clause of that predicate is null-guarded ahead of any comparison, so the predicate evaluates true or false and no row is absent from both views.

clauses.subject: defensive-projection
clauses.statement: A column a store may not carry is projected as the null literal, so a row missing it moves to the audit view instead of erroring the view out for every reader.

clauses.subject: step-output
clauses.statement: A journaled step runs its effect exactly once. The first call under a key enters the effect and durably writes what it produced; every later call under that key returns the written value without entering the effect again.

clauses.subject: entry-key
clauses.statement: A journal entry is keyed by `(execution_id, step_label, input_hash)`, which is the primary key of the `journal` table. An unfinished attempt reuses its execution id, so a second attempt resolves recorded work rather than writing a second copy of it.

clauses.subject: inline-cutoff
clauses.statement: A journaled value of 1 MiB or smaller lives inline in its row, bound as bytes so any codec round-trips it unchanged.

clauses.subject: value-tier
clauses.statement: Above the inline cutoff the value lands in a content-addressed file named by its sha256 under the blob directory and the row holds that reference. A caller receives bytes either way and branches on neither tier.

clauses.subject: blob-address
clauses.statement: A blob writer stages its own temporary file and renames it over the destination. The last rename wins and every outcome is the same file, since the destination name is the hash of its contents. No writer errors on another's in-flight write and none waits for one.

clauses.subject: missing-blob
clauses.statement: A row holding a blob reference whose file resolves to nothing fails with `BlobMissing` carrying the reference — never a panic, never an empty value standing in for the recorded one.

clauses.subject: row-admission
clauses.statement: Two writers racing one unwritten key may both compute. Admission is insert-or-ignore, one row survives, and the re-read hands the surviving value to both. The database lock releases before an effect runs, so an effect holds no catalog write lock.

clauses.subject: effect-boundary
clauses.statement: The determinism boundary is the journal. A body replays faithfully when every observable side effect passes through a recorded step, a cursor commit or an awakeable; the connector pull, the cursor commit and the snapshot commit are each such a step, and the work between them is pure.

clauses.subject: recorded-batch
clauses.statement: A journaled pull records the batch as the source handed it over, serialized inside the pull and ahead of the land path. The recorded artifact is a second envelope over the same rows rather than a copy of what the destination table ends up holding.

clauses.subject: replay-lands
clauses.statement: A journal hit hands back the recorded batch and the land path runs over it as it ran the first time, so a peppered mask applies once per landing and a resumed run lands bytes identical to an uninterrupted one. The resolved batch ordinal freezes into the artifact and survives shredding into parent and child tables.

clauses.subject: ledger-settles-first
clauses.statement: The outbound request ledger settles durably ahead of the entry that commits. A recorded batch can never exist without the set of vendor calls that produced it.

clauses.subject: removable-value
clauses.statement: No value a policy strips reaches the journal. Ordering holds that where ordering reaches, and where it does not the pairing that defeats it is refused ahead of the first pull, so nothing is written down and regretted.

clauses.subject: journaling-opt-out
clauses.statement: Pull journaling defaults on. A source opts out when its pre-pull cursor cannot name the content it is about to read, and the opt-out set is one constant pinned against each source's own declaration by a test. An empty pull is journaled under no circumstances.

clauses.subject: redacting-source
clauses.statement: A pipeline declaring write-path redaction over a source that journals its pulls raises `JournalRedactionConflict` ahead of its first pull — from the connector name during manifest validation, on the apply and reconcile path, and from the built source at run open, which also catches a source wired under a name no table declares.

clauses.subject: escape-hatch
clauses.statement: Two escape hatches exist and no third: `journal.unsafe(label, effect)` for an idempotent read where recording is pure overhead, and a source declaring that it journals no pull, which repeats that one source's pull on replay. Each carries a stated idempotency argument at a greppable call site.

clauses.subject: substrate-port
clauses.statement: The run-path substrate is reached through one interface: start or resume a run for a content-hashed plan reference, record a step's output, commit a cursor under its kind, suspend on an awakeable with a timeout, attach a retry schedule to a step, and describe the driver's capabilities.

clauses.subject: plan-pin
clauses.statement: The plan reference a run starts against is its replay pin. A run resolves the same plan for the whole of its life and never swaps to a mutated one mid-flight.

clauses.subject: unwired-capability
clauses.statement: A capability the running profile does not wire raises `CapabilityUnwired` when a caller reaches for it, so a profile mismatch fails on the first reach rather than inside a half-finished run.

clauses.subject: rebuild-survival
clauses.statement: Journal rows and execution ownership survive a readable rebuild of the catalog unchanged. Neither is reconstructed from the file tree after the catalog is lost, so a lost catalog is lost recorded work rather than recoverable work.

clauses.subject: cursor-kind
